Thomas Cajetan
tŏm´as kăj´e-tan
n. (Tommaso de Vio, 1469–1534, called Cajetan, Dominican cardinal and the greatest Thomist of his age, who examined Luther at Augsburg in 1518)
Latin Caietanus, of Gaeta, his birthplace; his religious name was Thomas, taken for Aquinas.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thomas Cajetan was a scholar of the first rank — his commentary on the Summa is still printed with it — and as papal legate he was sent to Augsburg in 1518 to secure Luther's submission. The interviews failed because of how they were framed: Cajetan was instructed not to dispute but to require recantation, and Luther asked to be shown from Scripture where he was wrong. That exchange is the Reformation in miniature. Isa 8:20 states Luther's demand — “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” — and Act 4:19 the apostolic precedent for refusing: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.” What makes Cajetan interesting is that he was himself a careful biblical scholar who, in his late commentaries, questioned the authorship of Hebrews, doubted the canonical standing of several books Rome would soon define at Trent, and preferred the Hebrew to the Vulgate. He was answering Luther with an authority he was privately subjecting to evidence.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to recant as to retract; to contradict a former declaration; and to prove as to try; to ascertain some unknown quality by experiment.

expand to see more

RECANT', v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration.

PROVE, v.t. To try; to ascertain some unknown quality or truth by an experiment, or by a test or standard.

2. To evince, establish or ascertain as truth, reality or fact, by argument, testimony or other evidence.

Key Scripture

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Act 4:19 — "But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye."

1Th 5:21 — "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."

Gal 2:6 — "But of these who seemed to be somewhat, (whatsoever they were, it maketh no matter to me: God accepteth no man's person:) for they who seemed to be somewhat in conference added nothing to me:"

Modern Corruption

Cajetan was told to demand a recantation rather than win an argument, and the instruction is the admission that the argument could not be won.

expand to see more

A church confident of its exegesis does not forbid its legate to dispute. The curial instruction at Augsburg was that Luther recant six words, not that he be refuted, and Cajetan — who could have argued with anyone in Europe — was reduced to repeating the demand. 1Th 5:21 is the method Scripture commands of the hearer: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good,” which presupposes that doctrine may be examined. Where examination is forbidden, authority has replaced truth as the ground of assent, and that substitution is the formal corruption the Reformation existed to undo.

Cajetan's private scholarship sharpens the point rather than softening it. He applied real critical judgment to the canon and the text, and would have been censured for it a generation later; Trent defined what he had left open. The recovery is the principle he was sent to deny and himself half practised: Isa 8:20 makes Scripture the standard by which every teacher, legate and council is measured, and Gal 2:6 says of the most eminent that “God accepteth no man's person.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew torah (H8451), law; teudah (H8584), testimony; Greek dokimazo (G1381), to prove, to test.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; Isaiah 8:20.

Hebrew teudah (H8584) — testimony, attestation; Isaiah 8:20.

Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to test, to prove; 1 Thessalonians 5:21.

Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold fast; 1 Thessalonians 5:21.

Greek prosopon (G4383) — a face, a person; Galatians 2:6.

Usage

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — Luther's demand at Augsburg."

"“Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19) — the apostolic precedent."

"“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21) — the method a recantation forbids."
